To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the variation of selected toxicant levels within commercial cigarettes is low (⩽15%) but higher for analytes present at low concentrations (⩾20%), and that the error associated with single point-in-time sampling of toxicant emissions is 2CV ∼ 20%.

(i) the variation in the levels of toxicants in the mainstream smoke of commercial cigarettes is high (up to 3.4-fold); (ii) the levels of toxicant emissions are highly variable (up to 2.7-fold) within a single product over time and (iii) this variability is greater for commercial cigarettes than for the 3R4f reference cigarette
The monthly variability of toxicant levels in the tobacco blend of commercial cigarettes was generally <15%.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the variation in the emissions of key toxicants in tobacco and mainstream cigarette smoke.
the variation of key toxicants in tobacco and smoke from commercial cigarettes.
the variation in the emissions of selected toxicants from tobacco and smoke of selected commercial cigarettes and the 3R4f reference cigarette.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a significant variation in the levels of toxicants in the smoke from different commercial cigarette products.

, in the absence of a standard reference cigarette, the variation in toxicant yields from commercial cigarette products is high, and that single-point-in-time toxicant measurements may not be sufficient to accurately reflect the toxicant levels of the product.
the variation of toxicant emissions in commercial cigarettes is high, and would be expected to be higher for low-level analytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the measurement of emissions from a commercial cigarette is associated with significant natural variation for low-level analytes, and that the error associated with single-point measurement is ∼ 20%.

, for a single laboratory, the variation associated with a single measurement is low, but that the variation associated with multiple measurements is higher and would be higher if measurements were conducted in more laboratories.
the variation is low enough to be useful, and that the variation can be reduced by reporting the emissions as a ratio of nicotine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single-point-in-time measurement of emissions from cigarettes is unlikely to provide a robust estimate of the emissions from the product.
single-point-in-time measurements are not sufficient for assessing the performance of commercial cigarette products.
the variation associated with single-point sampling and measurement of toxicants is high enough to make it difficult to determine whether the emissions have changed over time.
